source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: Experts recall random (shuffled) domain material better than novices, across domains. This supports small chunks, since random material has no large structure and no whole.
numbers: Random-effects r = .41, 95% CI [.29,.51], k = 28 samples, 903 participants, 24 studies; I2 = 63%. Dropping 2 flawed samples: r = .39, k = 26.
limits: Small samples. Mostly short exposures. Expertise was group-coded outside chess. Memory-training experts (mnemonists) were excluded.
agent_relevance: Small stored units explain part of expert advantage, so a subgoal library should hold many small reusable pieces, not only big schemas.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: The random-material effect shrinks after publication-bias correction, and music is an outlier explained by low randomness of the material.
numbers: Trim-and-fill (8 studies trimmed): r = .29, 95% CI [.17,.41]; fail-safe N = 745. By domain: games .42 (k=11), music .69 (k=5), programming .36 (k=6), sports .30 (k=3, CI includes 0), other .24 (k=3, CI includes 0). Domain moderator Q(4)=8.69, p=.069. Exposure time (8 s or less vs more) not a moderator, Q(1)=0.89, p=.346.
limits: Domain moderator only marginal. Sports and other were not significant alone. Music tasks used 5 notes on a stave, so the material was barely random.
agent_relevance: Expect a real but modest effect (r about .3). Do not credit a chunk library with large gains on unstructured input.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: The direction of the random-material skill effect is almost always positive.
numbers: 49 of 55 experiments (45 studies, 1,401 participants) had experts better than novices; binomial p = 9.1e-10 against 50/50.
limits: Direction only, no effect size. Includes underpowered studies.
agent_relevance: Consistent sign across domains supports chunking over holistic or schema-only accounts, which predict no effect.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: Re-analysis of 13 chess experiments (presentation 3 to 10 s) shows stronger players keep a small edge on random positions. The classic 'no edge' claim came from Chase and Simon (1973) with three players.
numbers: Strongest group beat weakest in 12 of 13 experiments, binomial p = .0017. Randomized-block ANOVA on skill F(3,17)=10.35, p<.001. Slope about 1 piece per 400 Elo on random positions vs about 5 pieces per 400 Elo on game positions. Reconstruction method (board, dictation, computer) no effect, F(2,27)=0.90.
limits: Most single studies were not significant (small N). Pooled by hand; no formal effect size because tests were not reported.
agent_relevance: Chunk advantage is mostly about structured material. The random-input gain is about one fifth of the structured gain.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of rapidly presented random chess positions is a function of skill
finding: The guessing explanation fails: strong players do not commit more errors of commission and do not guess better.
numbers: Errors of commission on random positions at 5 s: Masters 2.4, Experts 5.5, Class A 3.9 (n.s.). In a 1 to 60 s presentation study, skill gaps existed at all times and were larger at long times; errors at 5 s were 1.0, 3.1, 3.4. Jongman (1968): no skill edge at guessing piece locations.
limits: Commission-error data come only from the authors' own lab.
agent_relevance: A rival account (strategic guessing) is ruled out for chess, so the effect is stored content, not response bias.

source: Chase & Simon (1973) Perception in chess (as reported in Gobet & Simon 1996 and Gobet 1998)
finding: The founding study found no skill difference on random positions at 5 s. Its Master did worse than the novice on random boards. N was three players.
numbers: N = 3 players (Master, Class A, beginner). Figures come from secondary reports; the 1973 paper was not opened.
limits: Tiny sample. 12 of 13 later experiments disagree on direction.
agent_relevance: The famous 'chunks vanish on random input' result is weaker than textbooks say. Read it as 'mostly shrink', not 'vanish'.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: Mirror-image reflection of real positions hurts recall, and hurts strong players more. So chunks are tied to specific pieces at specific squares, as chunking and template theory say, not to abstract gist.
numbers: N = 25 players (5 Masters mean Elo 2395, 11 Experts 2146, 9 Class A 1890). Normal + horizontal-flip positions: 77.3%, 49.7%, 34.5% correct (Masters, Experts, Class A). Vertical + central flips: 62.9%, 38.6%, 27.5%. Contrast F(1,22)=96.79, p<.001. Skill x modification F(2,22)=3.48, p<.05. Simulation supports the usual estimate of about 50,000 chunks for Masters.
limits: A flip around the vertical axis also changes castling and king-side meaning, so some of the drop may be semantic. The simulation fit is indirect for the 50,000 figure.
agent_relevance: Key library entries to their context. A helper retrieved on surface form fails when the layout shifts.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Recall of random and distorted chess positions: implications for the theory of expertise
finding: On random positions the largest chunk and chunk count stay flat across skill. Skill differences in chunks appear only for game positions.
numbers: Largest chunk, game positions: Masters 11.2, Experts 7.4, Class A 6.2 pieces. Random positions: 4.1, 4.3, 4.1. Chunks per position, game: 4.0, 4.3, 2.5; random: 1.2, 1.7, 1.8. Skill effect on random pieces correct not significant, F(2,22)=0.18.
limits: Small groups (5, 11, 9).
agent_relevance: Chunking power depends on structure being present. Measure library gain on structured vs shuffled tasks to show it comes from chunk use.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) Templates in chess memory: a mechanism for recalling several boards
finding: Strong players exceed the 7 plus or minus 2 chunk limit when several boards are shown. This broke the original Chase-Simon capacity assumption and led to templates (large chunks with open slots).
numbers: N = 13 (3 Masters, 4 Experts, 6 Class A). Random positions at 5 s: Masters 21%, Experts 16%, Class A 12% (F(2,10)=3.46, ns). Up to 5 boards: Masters placed up to 60 pieces, Experts about 40. Chunks rose from 2.3 (1 board) to 9.9 (5 boards) for Experts and Masters; some individuals reached 13 to 15. Largest chunk 19.7 pieces (Masters, 1 board) falling to 12.4 with several boards. Recall correlated with time per board, r = .90 to .94.
limits: Chunks defined by 2 s placement gaps. N small. One Grandmaster lost attention in the 5-board trial, lowering Master means.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a library of slot-filling templates, not fixed snippets: larger units with variable parts held more.

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Expert chess memory: revisiting the chunking hypothesis
finding: Partial replication of the Chase-Simon chunk analysis with a computer display. The 2 s boundary and the chess-relation pattern replicate. Master chunks are much larger than in 1973.
numbers: N = 26 (5 Masters, 9 Experts, 12 Class A). Masters' mean of median largest chunk 16.8 pieces in recall and 14 in copy, vs 7 pieces for the 1973 Master. Random positions: largest chunk 6.3 (copy) and 4.6 (recall), flat across skill. Authors state exact replications are rare in chess psychology.
limits: Not exact: computer screen instead of physical pieces. The 1973 comparison rests on one Master, with no error bars.
agent_relevance: The chunk-boundary method holds up, but chunk size is not stable across setups. Test any 'ideal chunk size' in our own setup.

source: Gobet & Clarkson (2004) Chunks in expert memory: evidence for the magical number four... or is it two?
finding: Display medium changes chunk size a lot. With a physical board, chunks look small, as in 1973. On a screen, Masters show chunks up to 15 pieces and at most about three chunks, which favours template theory over chunking theory and over Cowan's four.
numbers: N = 12 (4 Masters, 4 Class B, 4 novices). Masters' median largest chunk, game positions: computer 14.8 (recall) and 12.9 (copy); physical board 7.5 and 3.8. Class B on computer: 9.0 and 7.8; novices 6.3 and 5.9. Display main effect F(1,9)=76.16, p<.001.
limits: Only 12 players. The three-chunk claim is for recall of one board.
agent_relevance: Chunk size is partly an artifact of how output is produced. Be careful measuring chunks from LLM output order or token limits.

source: Gong, Ericsson & Moxley (2015) Recall of briefly presented chess positions and its relation to chess skill
finding: A new independent chunk method (repeated recall) plus a non-player control group show large expertise effects in chunks for game positions only. It partly replicates and partly departs from Chase-Simon.
numbers: N = 25 rated players (USCF 411 to 2166, mean 1680) and 25 non-players. Chunk agreement across trials 93%. Number of chunks, game: 2.74 vs 1.02 (p<.001). Largest chunk, game: 4.56 vs 2.60 (p<.001). Random: 2.64 vs 2.08 largest chunk and 1.30 vs 0.98 chunks, not significant. Within players, largest game chunk vs rating r = .60 (p<.01). Within-chunk chess relations did not differ overall (2.81 vs 2.66).
limits: Players were club level (top group Expert, not Master). The random-position skill effect from the meta-analysis was not detected here. Chunks are smaller than in Gobet and Simon 1998.
agent_relevance: Chunk size scales with skill; largest chunk is the clearest marker. A candidate metric for library growth.

source: Gong, Ericsson & Moxley (2015) Recall of briefly presented chess positions and its relation to chess skill
finding: Rival account in the introduction: experts encode abstract relations, not location-specific chunks. The result depends on the task instructions.
numbers: Linhares and Brum found skilled players categorised positions by abstract relations. Bilalic and Gobet replied that participants did so because they were told to. Linhares and Brum replied that experts can and novices cannot. Gong et al. found only attack and defence relations separated players from non-players.
limits: This is the paper's own account; the original exchange was not opened.
agent_relevance: Keep two layers: surface chunks for fast match and abstract schema for gist. Evidence says surface chunks do the first work.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
finding: Random positions are the test that separates four theories. Chunking and template theory predict a small expert edge, SEEK (high-level schemas) predicts none, and long-term working memory with a square retrieval structure predicts a much larger edge than observed.
numbers: At 5 s on random positions Masters place about 5.5 pieces vs 2.6 for players below Class B. The LT-WM square version predicts an edge much stronger than the data; the LT-WM hierarchy version fits but then acts like chunking.
limits: Review by a chunking-theory author; relies on his own reading of the studies.
agent_relevance: Which theory is right matters for design: small-chunk library, retrieval structure, or schema.

source: Gobet (1998) Expert memory: a comparison of four theories
finding: Converging evidence for chunks as real units, and a boundary: random legal move sequences keep recall, random illegal ones destroy it.
numbers: Presenting pieces in chunk order at 2 s per piece beat column order and random order (Charness 1974; Frey & Adesman 1976), and beat showing the whole position for equal total time. Saariluoma: recall of random LEGAL games fell to about 60% after 25 moves vs about 90% for real games; random illegal games under 20%. Chase-Simon: 25-piece middlegames recalled better than 13-piece endgames; Saariluoma (1984) replicated with 5, 15, 20, 25 pieces.
limits: Secondary summary; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Order and grouping of inputs change what is retained. Legal-looking noise still holds chunks, so test on truly scrambled inputs.

source: Gathercole et al. (2019) Can short-term memory be trained? (also reports Ericsson, Chase & Faloon 1980 and Chase & Ericsson 1981)
finding: S.F. raised digit span from 7 to 79 over two years by recoding digits into running times. The gain did not carry over to letters. A second runner, D.D., copied the strategy and also gained.
numbers: S.F.: span 7 to 79 digits; letter span stayed 7. Martin and Fernberger (1929): span up about 40% with grouping.
limits: 1980 and 1981 papers not opened; numbers come from this 2019 article that cites them. N = 1, then N = 2.
agent_relevance: Chunk gains are tied to material the recoder already knows. A library helps only where matching codes exist.

source: Gathercole et al. (2019) Can short-term memory be trained? (also reports Ericsson, Chase & Faloon 1980 and Chase & Ericsson 1981)
finding: 20 sessions of adaptive digit-span training raised trained span but did not transfer to spoken digits or letters. Colour-change training transferred only to a similar visual task.
numbers: Visual digit span, trained digits group: 406 to 659 (d about 1.60). Letter span group effect p = .300 (no transfer). Spoken digit span p = .044. Colour-change training transferred to line orientation.
quote: training only generates substantial transfer when the unfamiliar demands of the training activities require the development of novel routines
limits: Per-group N not extracted. Four groups: digits, circles, colour, no training.
agent_relevance: Gains stay inside the task type. Do not claim library benefits transfer.

source: Fingerprint examiners study (2024) The effect of fingerprint expertise on visual short-term memory
finding: Outside games: fingerprint experts beat novices on visual short-term memory for fingerprints, and still did after print distinctiveness was manipulated.
numbers: 44 examiners (mean 14.9 years) vs 44 matched novices. Speed-accuracy score t(86)=8.23, p<.001, d = 1.76. Years of experience vs accuracy in experts: r(42) = 0.01.
limits: Experience did not predict performance, so the gap may be selection or training rather than dose. No random-material control.
agent_relevance: An expert memory edge can be large inside a trained domain without scaling with time spent.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Cognitive mechanisms underlying memory advantages in bridge experts
finding: Bridge experts' hand memory depends on grouping cards by suit (visual familiarity) and on abstract knowledge. Results support chunking/template theory and SEEK together.
numbers: Experiment 1: the suit-categorisation rule mattered for recognition and free recall; the rank-order rule did not (honor cards did). Experiment 2: visual familiarity drove recognition; familiarity plus abstract knowledge drove recall. Test statistics not extracted.
limits: Experts were national masters in China (10+ years, 10,000+ hours). Sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: A hybrid view: surface chunks plus abstract rules. Design the library with both.

source: Expert brain study (2026) Low-dimensional and optimised representations of high-level information in the expert brain, Nature Communications
finding: fMRI in chess: experts' codes are more compact, more relational and sit in frontoparietal rather than sensory cortex. The authors read this as supporting and extending chunking and template theories.
numbers: 20 experts (mean Elo 2036, SD 147) vs 20 novices (19 and 20 in the behavioural model comparison). Within experts, Elo vs checkmate RSA model fit r = .47, p = .039, CI [.03,.75].
limits: Small N, cross-sectional, checkmate evaluation rather than recall. The chunking reading is the authors'.
agent_relevance: Expertise looks like compression toward relational features: store compact relational helpers, not raw traces.

source: Modelling working memory capacity: is the magical number four, seven, or does it depend on what you are counting? (2024) Journal of Cognition
finding: Capacity estimates depend on presentation time: long presentation gives higher capacity, read as recoding or chunking. Short displays give a lower number.
numbers: Experiments 2 and 3: 5000 ms vs 120 ms visual array; k higher with long presentation. The CSVI estimate was about one unit above the short visual array task.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read closely; sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: The 4 vs 7 gap is largely chunking opportunity, so think of context limits in chunks, not raw items.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: A skill library of executable code is a chunk store for an LLM agent. Removing it makes progress plateau late.
numbers: Versus prior SOTA: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distance, tech milestones up to 15.3x faster. Ablations: random curriculum -93% items; no self-verification -73%; GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4 gives 5.7x fewer items. No-library curve plateaus (text gives no number; read from a figure).
limits: One environment (Minecraft). Library ablation shown only as a plot. Effects overlap with the curriculum.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of our subgoal library. The library pays off late and by compounding, not early.

source: Berlot-Attwell et al. (2024) Library learning doesn't: the curious case of the single-use library
finding: Failed-replication style result: LLM library-learning gains in math are not caused by reuse. Learned items are almost never reused; self-correction and self-consistency explain the gain.
numbers: LEGO-Prover: over 20,000 lemmas learned, 1,233 (6%) entered the final prover prompt, exactly one was reused (once). A zero-reuse ablation performed similarly. TroVE on MATH: final libraries had 15 learned functions and 3 successful reuses in 3,201 test questions. TroVE library learning often lowered performance.
limits: Two systems, math only (miniF2F and MATH).
agent_relevance: Strong warning. Audit actual reuse, not only final accuracy. Track reuse counts as a measured outcome.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows (routines) from past trajectories raises web-agent success. Online induction transfers to new sites and domains.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4): +12.0 points absolute, 51.1% relative over BrowserGym; about 2.0 fewer steps per task; 7.6% relative above SteP with human-written workflows. Mind2Web: 24.6% relative. Gains of 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points as train-test shift widens.
limits: Benchmarks only; no reuse-rate audit like Berlot-Attwell et al.
agent_relevance: Routine-sized chunks help when matched to the task template. Test template match explicitly.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: Retrieved thought-templates distilled from earlier solutions improve reasoning accuracy and cut cost.
numbers: Abstract only: +11% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One across 10 tasks; about 12% of the cost of multi-query methods.
limits: Abstract only. Authors' own results, not independently replicated. Same reuse-audit concern as Berlot-Attwell et al.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our 'template' idea. Needs a reuse audit before trust.

source: Gong et al. (2023) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study
finding: ChatGPT shows a working-memory limit in n-back tasks resembling humans. Instruction strategy does not remove the limit pattern.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers extracted.
limits: Not a chunking test. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: A capacity limit exists in context use; chunking is the human way around it.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent world models and latent variable estimation in Chess-playing language models
finding: A character-level GPT trained on real chess games forms internal board-state representations (linear probes) that can be steered. Not a chunk test.
numbers: Abstract only; numbers not extracted.
limits: No random-position vs game recall test for LLMs was found in the sources checked. Search tools were rate-limited, so such a study may exist unseen.
agent_relevance: Open gap: no direct LLM test of the game vs random recall asymmetry was found. A cheap probe we could run ourselves.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder; Grand et al. (2023) LILO
finding: Library learning by compression: find shared abstractions across solved programs and add them as primitives. LILO adds LLM synthesis and auto-documentation, which helps the LLM deploy them.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers extracted.
limits: Abstract only. Berlot-Attwell et al. suggest LLM library gains can come from other sources.
agent_relevance: A formal basis for choosing what becomes a chunk: compress repeated structure, then name it.
